- DFS is a traversal algorithm commonly used to search for elements in graphs or trees. It explores a path as far as possible before backtracking and exploring other paths. DFS can be implemented recursively or using a stack.

- BFS is another traversal algorithm used for searching in graphs or trees. It explores all the neighboring elements at the current depth level before moving to the next depth level. BFS can be implemented using a queue.

- Hashing is a technique used to efficiently search for elements in hash tables or associative arrays. It uses a hash function to map keys to specific positions in the data structure, allowing for constant-time retrieval of values..

- To achieve sorting in Bubble Sort, the adjacent elements in the array are compared and the positions are swapped if the first element is greater than the second. In this fashion, the largest value 'bubbles' to the top.
- Usually, after each iteration the elements furthest to the right are in correct order. The process is repeated until all the elements are in their right position.

- Selection sort divides the input array into a sorted and an unsorted region. It repeatedly selects the smallest element from the unsorted region and swaps it with the leftmost element of the unsorted region. Selection sort has a time complexity of O(n^2) in all cases..

- Insertion sort builds the final sorted array one element at a time. It iterates through the array and inserts each element into its correct position within the sorted portion of the array. Insertion sort has a time complexity of O(n^2) in the average and worst cases but performs well on small or nearly sorted arrays.

- Merge sort follows the divide-and-conquer approach. It divides the input array into two halves, recursively sorts them, and then merges the two sorted halves to produce a sorted output. Merge sort has a time complexity of O(n log n) in all cases and is a stable sorting algorithm.

- Quick sort also follows the divide-and-conquer approach. It selects a pivot element, partitions the array around the pivot, and recursively sorts the subarrays created by the partition. Quick sort has an average time complexity of O(n log n), but its worst-case time complexity is O(n^2) (which can be mitigated using various optimizations)
